Germany. A major European nation at the crossroads of Central and Western Europe, whose history spans from tribal kingdoms through the fragmented Holy Roman Empire to modern statehood. Its culture has profoundly shaped Western philosophy, music, literature, and science. Politically, Germany's twentieth-century history—the rise of Prussian militarism, the devastation of the World Wars, and Nazi tyranny—repeatedly altered the continent and world.

Germany was fragmented into hundreds of semi-independent states within the Holy Roman Empire from eight forty-three to eighteen zero six until Otto von Bismarck unified Prussia and surrounding territories into a single nation-state between eighteen sixty-four and eighteen seventy-one. The Protestant Reformation, initiated by Martin Luther in fifteen seventeen when he challenged papal authority, began in Germany and reshaped European Christianity, governance, and culture. Germany's culture produced philosophical giants like Goethe, Schiller, Kant, and Hegel and musical masters like Bach, Mozart, and Beethoven who defined Enlightenment and Romantic thought and sound.

Prussian militarism under Bismarck and his successors made Germany an aggressive power. German imperial ambitions contributed to World War One from nineteen fourteen to nineteen eighteen, which devastated Europe. The Treaty of Versailles imposed harsh reparations and territorial losses on Germany after World War One, creating economic and political instability that fueled the rise of Adolf Hitler and the Nazi regime. World War Two, initiated by Nazi Germany from nineteen thirty-nine to nineteen forty-five, resulted in the Holocaust and the deaths of over seventy million people. Germany's defeat divided the nation into East and West until nineteen ninety.

Germany's cultural contributions to music, philosophy, and literature remain unmatched. It was also a center of scientific innovation where Einstein, Max Planck, and Marie Curie worked.
